claim: A missense mutation in the human Cryptochrome 2 (CRY2) gene co-segregates with Familial Advanced Sleep Phase (FASP) in one family.
source: We identified a missense mutation in the human Cryptochrome 2 (CRY2) gene that co-segregates with FASP in one family.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding directly in the abstract and results section, supported by pedigree analysis and sequencing data.

claim: The CRY2 mutation leads to replacement of an alanine residue at position 260 with a threonine (A260T).
source: The mutation leads to replacement of an alanine residue at position 260 with a threonine (A260T).
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1A with sequencing data.

claim: In mice, the CRY2 mutation causes a shortened circadian period.
source: In mice, the CRY2 mutation causes a shortened circadian period and reduced phase-shift to early-night light pulse associated with phase-advanced behavioral rhythms in the light-dark cycle.
evidence: Behavioral analysis of transgenic mice showed shortened free-running period as documented in Figure 2F.

claim: In mice, the CRY2 mutation causes reduced phase-shift to early-night light pulse.
source: In mice, the CRY2 mutation causes a shortened circadian period and reduced phase-shift to early-night light pulse associated with phase-advanced behavioral rhythms in the light-dark cycle.
evidence: Phase-shift experiments shown in Figure 2E demonstrate reduced phase-delay response to light at ZT14.

claim: In mice, the CRY2 mutation is associated with phase-advanced behavioral rhythms in the light-dark cycle.
source: In mice, the CRY2 mutation causes a shortened circadian period and reduced phase-shift to early-night light pulse associated with phase-advanced behavioral rhythms in the light-dark cycle.
evidence: Figure 2A-C show advanced peak time of resting behavior and activity offset in mutant mice.

claim: The A260T mutation is located in the phosphate loop of the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) binding domain of CRY2.
source: The A260T mutation is located in the phosphate loop of the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) binding domain of CRY2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and illustrated in Figure 1B showing the domain structure.

claim: The A260T mutation alters the conformation of CRY2.
source: The mutation alters the conformation of CRY2, increasing its accessibility and affinity for FBXL3 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase), thus promoting its degradation.
evidence: Structural modeling in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and biochemical assays support conformational changes.

claim: The A260T mutation increases CRY2 accessibility and affinity for FBXL3.
source: The mutation alters the conformation of CRY2, increasing its accessibility and affinity for FBXL3 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase), thus promoting its degradation.
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5E show increased binding of mutant CRY2 to FBXL3.

claim: The A260T mutation promotes CRY2 degradation.
source: The mutation alters the conformation of CRY2, increasing its accessibility and affinity for FBXL3 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase), thus promoting its degradation.
evidence: Degradation assays in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A show faster degradation of mutant CRY2.

claim: CRY2 stability controlled by FBXL3 plays a key role in the regulation of human sleep wake behavior.
source: These results demonstrate that CRY2 stability controlled by FBXL3 plays a key role in the regulation of human sleep wake behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined human genetic and mouse model data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Familial Advanced Sleep Phase (FASP) is a heritable human sleep phenotype characterized by very early sleep and wake times.
source: Familial Advanced Sleep Phase (FASP) is a heritable sleep phenotype characterized by stable early sleep and wake times (Jones et al., 1999; Reid and Burgess, 2005; Reid et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a definition supported by cited literature.

claim: The circadian clock is composed of interlocked transcriptional and translational negative feedback loops.
source: The circadian clock is composed of interlocked transcriptional and translational negative feedback loops (Lowrey and Takahashi, 2004; Reppert and Weaver, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, a CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer binds to E-boxes and activates gene expression of the Period (Per) and Cryptochrome (Cry) genes.
source: In mammals, a CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimer binds to E-boxes and activates gene expression of the Period (Per) and Cryptochrome (Cry) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: Translated PERs and CRYs proteins form a complex that enters the nucleus to inhibit their own transcription through direct interaction with CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimers.
source: Translated PERs and CRYs proteins form a complex that enters the nucleus to inhibit their own transcription through direct interaction with CLOCK-BMAL1 heterodimers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: CRY2 is a principal component in mammalian circadian clocks.
source: CRY2 is a principal component in mammalian circadian clocks (Shearman et al., 2000; van der Horst et al., 1999; Vitaterna et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Drosophila and plant CRY proteins act as photoreceptors contributing to photoentrainment of the circadian clock by binding to flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).
source: While Drosophila and plant CRY proteins act as photoreceptors contributing to photoentrainment of the circadian clock and other biological processes by binding to flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) (Partch and Sancar, 2005), mammalian CRY2 has light-independent transcriptional repressor activity and strongly inhibits E-box-regulated gene expression (Griffin et al., 1999; Kume et al., 1999; Shearman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Mammalian CRY2 has light-independent transcriptional repressor activity and strongly inhibits E-box-regulated gene expression.
source: While Drosophila and plant CRY proteins act as photoreceptors contributing to photoentrainment of the circadian clock and other biological processes by binding to flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) (Partch and Sancar, 2005), mammalian CRY2 has light-independent transcriptional repressor activity and strongly inhibits E-box-regulated gene expression (Griffin et al., 1999; Kume et al., 1999; Shearman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: FBXL3 is an F-box type E3 ubiquitin ligase which promotes CRY1 and CRY2 ubiquitylation thus leading to proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: Among them, FBXL3 is an F-box type E3 ubiquitin ligase which promotes CRY1 and CRY2 ubiquitylation thus leading to proteasome-mediated degradation (Busino et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Mutations in mouse Fbxl3 or knockout of the Fbxl3 gene dramatically lengthens the period of mouse behavioral rhythms in constant darkness.
source: Mutations in mouse Fbxl3 or knockout of the Fbxl3 gene dramatically lengthens the period of mouse behavioral rhythms in constant darkness (Godinho et al., 2007; Hirano et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Siepka et al., 2007), indicating that the protein stability of CRY1 and CRY2 is a critical determinant of circadian period in mice.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The protein stability of CRY1 and CRY2 is a critical determinant of circadian period in mice.
source: Mutations in mouse Fbxl3 or knockout of the Fbxl3 gene dramatically lengthens the period of mouse behavioral rhythms in constant darkness (Godinho et al., 2007; Hirano et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Siepka et al., 2007), indicating that the protein stability of CRY1 and CRY2 is a critical determinant of circadian period in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on Fbxl3 mutations.

claim: The FASP phenotype can segregate as a highly penetrant, autosomal dominant trait in human kindreds.
source: The FASP phenotype can segregate as a highly penetrant, autosomal dominant trait in human kindreds.
evidence: This is stated based on previous studies and the pedigree analysis in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutations in clock genes, including Period2, Period3, casein kinase Iδ, and Dec2 cause circadian and sleep homeostasis phenotypes in humans.
source: Previously, we have identified mutations in clock genes, including Period2, Period3, casein kinase Iδ, and Dec2 causing circadian and sleep homeostasis phenotypes in humans (He et al., 2009; Toh et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: A mutation at the phosphorylation priming site of PER2 attenuates sequential phosphorylation and consequently destabilizes PER2 proteins.
source: A mutation at the phosphorylation priming site of PER2 attenuates sequential phosphorylation and consequently destabilizes PER2 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The mouse model expressing mutant PER2 exhibits a shortened circadian period accompanied with large phase-advance in sleep-wake rhythms.
source: The mouse model expressing mutant PER2 exhibits a shortened circadian period accompanied with large phase-advance in sleep-wake rhythms (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: No other novel mutations were found in ~25 candidate circadian genes that were sequenced in the FASP family.
source: No other novel mutations were found in ~25 candidate circadian genes that were sequenced.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the mutation screening.

claim: The fraternal twin sisters inherited the mutation from their mother and both reported a strong morning preference (Horne-Ostberg scores of 84 and 72).
source: The fraternal twin sisters inherited the mutation from their mother and both reported a strong morning preference (Horne-Ostberg scores of 84 and 72) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to source data.

claim: The proband had a very early melatonin onset (4:41 P.M.), while the averaged melatonin onset of normative samples is 8:50 P.M.
source: The proband also had a very early melatonin onset (4:41 P.M.), while the averaged melatonin onset of normative samples is 8:50 P.M. (Burgess and Fogg, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with comparison to normative data from cited literature.

claim: The proband's melatonin onset time is 3.35 standard deviations earlier than expected and among the earliest 0.05% of normative samples.
source: Her melatonin onset time is 3.35 standard deviations earlier than expected and among the earliest 0.05% of normative samples (Burgess and Fogg, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to normative data.

claim: Ala260 is highly conserved in CRY1 and CRY2 proteins of various species.
source: Ala260 is located in the FAD binding domain of CRY2 and it is highly conserved in CRY1 and CRY2 proteins of various species (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the amino acid alignment in Figure 1B.

claim: Under conditions of 12 hr light and 12 hr dark (LD 12:12), both hCRY2-WT and hCRY2-A260T mice entrained stably to the LD cycle.
source: Under conditions of 12 hr light and 12 hr dark (LD 12:12), both hCRY2-WT and hCRY2-A260T mice entrained stably to the LD cycle (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The peak time of resting behavior was significantly advanced in hCRY2-A260T mutant mice compared to hCRY2-WT mice.
source: However, the peak time of resting behavior, as determined by quadratic-function fitting, was significantly advanced in hCRY2-A260T mutant mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance.

claim: The activity offset and onset times were advanced in hCRY2-A260T mutant mice vs. hCRY2-WT mice.
source: The activity offset and onset times were also advanced in hCRY2-A260T mutant mice vs. hCRY2-WT mice (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: hCRY2-A260T mutant mice on a Cry2 null background demonstrated advanced activity onset and offset, especially around the LD transition (ZT12-13).
source: Similarly, hCRY2-A260T mutant mice on a Cry2 null background demonstrated advanced activity onset and offset, especially around the LD transition (ZT12-13) (Figure 2-—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: hCRY2-A260T mice recapitulate the advanced sleep phase seen in the human FASP subjects harboring the CRY2 mutation.
source: These results demonstrate that hCRY2-A260T mice recapitulate the advanced sleep phase seen in the human FASP subjects harboring the CRY2 mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in mice.

claim: hCRY2-A260T showed reduced phase-delay when mice were subjected to a 30-min light pulse at ZT14.
source: Interestingly, hCRY2-A260T showed reduced phase-delay when mice were subjected to a 30-min light pulse at ZT14 (Figure 2D,E), whereas phase-advance was normal in response to a light pulse at ZT22 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Phase-advance was normal in hCRY2-A260T mice in response to a light pulse at ZT22.
source: Interestingly, hCRY2-A260T showed reduced phase-delay when mice were subjected to a 30-min light pulse at ZT14 (Figure 2D,E), whereas phase-advance was normal in response to a light pulse at ZT22 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutant mice have reduced sensitivity to entrainment by light at early night compared to control mice.
source: Thus, mutant mice have reduced sensitivity to entrainment by light at early night compared to control mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced phase-delay at ZT14.

claim: The free-running period of hCRY2-A260T (23.52±0.04 hr) was significantly shorter than that of hCRY2-WT (23.70±0.03 hr) and WT mice (23.74±0.02 hr).
source: The free-running period of hCRY2-A260T (23.52±0.04 hr) was significantly shorter than that of hCRY2-WT (23.70±0.03 hr) and WT mice (23.74±0.02 hr) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific values and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The period shortening phenotype was further enhanced by crossing Tg mice onto the mCry2 null background.
source: The period shortening phenotype was further enhanced by crossing Tg mice onto the mCry2 null background (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The shorter circadian period and reduced phase-delay were also observed in another mutant line (23.51±0.06 hr) with a higher mutant transgene copy number.
source: The shorter circadian period and reduced phase-delay were also observed in another mutant line (23.51±0.06 hr) with a higher mutant transgene copy number (Figure 2—figure supplements 1A, 4B), thus excluding the possibility that the phenotype was due to positional effects of the transgene insertion site in the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There is no significant difference in the periods and phase-shifting of hCRY2-WT transgenic vs. transgene negative mice.
source: Of note, there is no significant difference in the periods and phase-shifting of hCRY2-WT transgenic vs. transgene negative mice (Figure 2E,F), indicating that the shortening of circadian period and abnormal phase-delay are not simply due to overexpression of hCRY2.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The shortening of circadian period and abnormal phase-delay are not simply due to overexpression of hCRY2.
source: Of note, there is no significant difference in the periods and phase-shifting of hCRY2-WT transgenic vs. transgene negative mice (Figure 2E,F), indicating that the shortening of circadian period and abnormal phase-delay are not simply due to overexpression of hCRY2.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of transgenic and non-transgenic mice.

claim: The phase-advances in mice and humans results from the CRY2 mutation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the phase-advances in mice and humans results from the CRY2 mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined human and mouse data.

claim: The phase advance may be due to a combination of shortened period and altered sensitivity to photic entrainment.
source: Data from the transgenic mice suggests that the phase advance may be due to a combination of shortened period and altered sensitivity to photic entrainment.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing both period shortening and altered phase-shifting.

claim: Shortened circadian period was observed in PER2::LUC bioluminescence rhythms of liver and lung cultures from hCRY2-A260T vs. WT mice.
source: Consistent with the behavioral rhythms, shortened clock period was observed in PER2::LUC bioluminescence rhythms of liver and lung cultures from hCRY2-A260T vs. WT mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The peak and trough time of the bioluminescence rhythms were advanced in both tissues of hCRY2-A260T mice.
source: The peak and trough time of the bioluminescence rhythms were advanced in both tissues of hCRY2-A260T mice, suggesting that phase of the peripheral clock is also advanced by the mutation in vivo (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phase of the peripheral clock is advanced by the mutation in vivo.
source: The peak and trough time of the bioluminescence rhythms were advanced in both tissues of hCRY2-A260T mice, suggesting that phase of the peripheral clock is also advanced by the mutation in vivo (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the advanced peak and trough times in peripheral tissues.

claim: Circadian period shortening by the A260T mutation was found using mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) derived from mice with a mutant vs. WT transgene on both WT and mCry2 knockout backgrounds.
source: Circadian period shortening by the A260T mutation was also found using mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) derived from mice with a mutant vs. WT transgene on both WT and mCry2 knockout backgrounds (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: NIH3T3 cells stably expressing CRY2-A260T displayed a shorter circadian period than CRY2-WT expressing cells.
source: In addition, NIH3T3 cells stably expressing CRY2-A260T also displayed a shorter circadian period than CRY2-WT expressing cells (Figure 3F), emphasizing the dominant effect of CRY2-A260T on the circadian period.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CRY2-A260T has a dominant effect on the circadian period.
source: In addition, NIH3T3 cells stably expressing CRY2-A260T also displayed a shorter circadian period than CRY2-WT expressing cells (Figure 3F), emphasizing the dominant effect of CRY2-A260T on the circadian period.
evidence: This is inferred from the period shortening in cells expressing the mutant protein.

claim: CRY2-A260T shortens the circadian period in both central and peripheral clocks.
source: Our results indicate that CRY2-A260T shortens the circadian period in both central and peripheral clocks, consistent with current understanding that core clock genes such as Cry2 influence physiologies in multiple mammalian organ systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and tissue culture data.

claim: Core clock genes such as Cry2 influence physiologies in multiple mammalian organ systems.
source: Our results indicate that CRY2-A260T shortens the circadian period in both central and peripheral clocks, consistent with current understanding that core clock genes such as Cry2 influence physiologies in multiple mammalian organ systems.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The CRY2 Ala260 residue resides in the 'phosphate loop' responsible for binding to the phosphate of FAD.
source: The CRY2 Ala260 residue resides in the 'phosphate loop' responsible for binding to the phosphate of FAD (Hitomi et al., 2009) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated with citation and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutations at amino acid residues critical for FAD binding affect CRY2 repressor activity of E-box-mediated transcriptional activation.
source: Mutations at amino acid residues critical for FAD binding affect CRY2 repressor activity of E-box-mediated transcriptional activation (Czarna et al., 2013; Hitomi et al., 2009; Sanada et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Ser265 of mouse CRY2 (homologous residue of Ser266 in human CRY2) is a phosphorylation site.
source: Furthermore, Ser265 of mouse CRY2 (homologous residue of Ser266 in human CRY2) is a phosphorylation site, and the S265D mutation, mimicking a phosphorylated serine 265, reduces CRY2 repressor activity (Sanada et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The S265D mutation, mimicking a phosphorylated serine 265, reduces CRY2 repressor activity.
source: Furthermore, Ser265 of mouse CRY2 (homologous residue of Ser266 in human CRY2) is a phosphorylation site, and the S265D mutation, mimicking a phosphorylated serine 265, reduces CRY2 repressor activity (Sanada et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The A260T mutation weakened CRY2 repressor activity on Per1 E-box-mediated transcriptional activation by CLOCK-BMAL1.
source: Using a Luciferase assay, we found that the A260T mutation weakened CRY2 repressor activity on Per1 E-box-mediated transcriptional activation by CLOCK-BMAL1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The nuclear CRY2 protein levels in culture cells were decreased by the mutation.
source: However, the nuclear CRY2 protein levels in culture cells were decreased by the mutation (Figure 4B), which could potentially account for the reduction of CRY2 repressor activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The decreased nuclear CRY2 protein levels could potentially account for the reduction of CRY2 repressor activity.
source: However, the nuclear CRY2 protein levels in culture cells were decreased by the mutation (Figure 4B), which could potentially account for the reduction of CRY2 repressor activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between protein levels and repressor activity.

claim: CRY2-A260T was less stable than CRY2-WT in HEK293 cells, especially in the nucleus.
source: Consistent with the cellular distribution of CRY2 (Figure 4B), CRY2-A260T was less stable than CRY2-WT in HEK293 cells, especially in the nucleus (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Destabilization of CRY2 by the mutation was verified in a CRY2-LUC based bioluminescence degradation assay.
source: Destabilization of CRY2 by the mutation was further verified in a CRY2-LUC based bioluminescence degradation assay, where the protein decay rate can be determined by recording CRY2-LUC bioluminescence in culture (Hirano et al., 2013; Hirota et al., 2012) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ala260 does not directly bind to FAD.
source: Although Ala260 does not directly bind to FAD (Hitomi et al., 2009), amino acid conversion from the hydrophobic and small amino acid, alanine, to threonine could alter the conformation of the phosphate loop.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Amino acid conversion from alanine to threonine could alter the conformation of the phosphate loop.
source: Although Ala260 does not directly bind to FAD (Hitomi et al., 2009), amino acid conversion from the hydrophobic and small amino acid, alanine, to threonine could alter the conformation of the phosphate loop.
evidence: This is inferred from the chemical properties of the amino acids.

claim: A mutation from alanine to aspartic acid (A260D) caused a more severe effect on CRY2 repressor activity and protein stability than the A260T mutation.
source: This idea is supported by an observation that a mutation from alanine to aspartic acid (A260D) caused a more severe effect on CRY2 repressor activity and protein stability than the A260T mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Human CRY1 harboring the corresponding mutation at position 241 is less stable than CRY1-WT.
source: We found that human CRY1 harboring the corresponding mutation at position 241 is less stable than CRY1-WT, suggesting a common regulatory mechanism for CRY1 and CRY2 by FAD binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a common regulatory mechanism for CRY1 and CRY2 by FAD binding.
source: We found that human CRY1 harboring the corresponding mutation at position 241 is less stable than CRY1-WT, suggesting a common regulatory mechanism for CRY1 and CRY2 by FAD binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar effects of corresponding mutations in CRY1 and CRY2.

claim: The conformation of the phosphate loop may play critical roles in regulating CRY2 stability and repressor activity.
source: These results indicate that the conformation of the phosphate loop may play critical roles in regulating CRY2 stability and repressor activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of mutations in the phosphate loop region.

claim: FBXL3 primarily localizes in the nucleus and promotes proteasomal degradation of CRY2.
source: FBXL3 primarily localizes in the nucleus and promotes proteasomal degradation of CRY2, consequently having a strong impact on the circadian period of mice (Busino et al., 2007; Godinho et al., 2007; Siepka et al., 2007; Stojkovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: FBXL3 has a strong impact on the circadian period of mice.
source: FBXL3 primarily localizes in the nucleus and promotes proteasomal degradation of CRY2, consequently having a strong impact on the circadian period of mice (Busino et al., 2007; Godinho et al., 2007; Siepka et al., 2007; Stojkovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: C-terminal region of FBXL3 interacts with CRY2 through the FAD binding pocket.
source: A previous structural study demonstrated that C-terminal region of FBXL3 interacts with CRY2 through the FAD binding pocket and mutations in the FAD binding domain alter CRY2-FBXL3 interaction (Xing et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Mutations in the FAD binding domain alter CRY2-FBXL3 interaction.
source: A previous structural study demonstrated that C-terminal region of FBXL3 interacts with CRY2 through the FAD binding pocket and mutations in the FAD binding domain alter CRY2-FBXL3 interaction (Xing et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: hFBXL3 knockdown in HEK293 cells increased the stability of both CRY2-WT and CRY2-A260T.
source: As anticipated, hFBXL3 knockdown in HEK293 cells increased the stability of both CRY2-WT and CRY2-A260T.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The destabilizing effect of the A260T mutation was abrogated by hFBXL3 knockdown.
source: Interestingly, the destabilizing effect of the A260T mutation was abrogated by hFBXL3 knockdown (Figure 5A), suggesting the effect of the mutation requires FBXL3.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of the A260T mutation requires FBXL3.
source: Interestingly, the destabilizing effect of the A260T mutation was abrogated by hFBXL3 knockdown (Figure 5A), suggesting the effect of the mutation requires FBXL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the FBXL3 knockdown experiment.

claim: FAD stabilizes CRY2 by structurally interfering with the interaction between FBXL3 and CRY2.
source: FAD stabilizes CRY2 by structurally interfering with the interaction between FBXL3 and CRY2 (Xing et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Treatment of HEK293 cells with FAD increased CRY2-WT protein levels much more than CRY2-A260T.
source: We found that treatment of HEK293 cells with FAD increased CRY2-WT protein levels much more than CRY2-A260T (Figure 5B), suggesting that stabilization of CRY2 by FAD was reduced by the mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stabilization of CRY2 by FAD was reduced by the A260T mutation.
source: We found that treatment of HEK293 cells with FAD increased CRY2-WT protein levels much more than CRY2-A260T (Figure 5B), suggesting that stabilization of CRY2 by FAD was reduced by the mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential response to FAD treatment.

claim: Free CRY2-WT protein levels increased with addition of FAD in a dose-dependent manner in the competitive assay.
source: Free CRY2-WT protein levels increased with addition of FAD in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutant CRY2 was released less readily than CRY2-WT from the CRY2-FBXL3 complexes even though both forms of CRY2 were bound to FBXL3 at the same level.
source: In contrast, mutant CRY2 was released less readily than CRY2-WT from the complexes even though both forms of CRY2 were bound to FBXL3 at the same level (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: KL001 is a small synthetic molecule known to stabilize CRY1 and CRY2 due to its structural similarity to FAD.
source: In addition, we tested FBXL3-mediated CRY2 degradation using KL001, a small synthetic molecule known to stabilize CRY1 and CRY2 (Hirota et al., 2012) due to its structural similarity to FAD (Nangle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: KL001 stabilizes CRY2-WT in a dose-dependent manner.
source: KL001 stabilizes CRY2-WT in a dose-dependent manner as was previously reported (Hirota et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: KL001 failed to stabilize CRY2-A260T to the same extent it did for CRY2-WT.
source: However, KL001 failed to stabilize CRY2-A260T to the same extent it did for CRY2-WT (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D and supplementary figures.

claim: The A260T mutation weakened the function of FAD and KL001 as inhibitors of FBXL3-mediated degradation of CRY2.
source: These results indicate that the A260T mutation weakened the function of FAD and KL001 as inhibitors of FBXL3-mediated degradation of CRY2 and that CRY2-A260T is less stable than CRY-WT, likely due to strengthened interaction with FBXL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the FAD and KL001 experiments.

claim: CRY2-A260T is less stable than CRY-WT, likely due to strengthened interaction with FBXL3.
source: These results indicate that the A260T mutation weakened the function of FAD and KL001 as inhibitors of FBXL3-mediated degradation of CRY2 and that CRY2-A260T is less stable than CRY-WT, likely due to strengthened interaction with FBXL3.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results.

claim: CRY2-A260T binds more strongly to FBXL3 than CRY2-WT in HEK293 cells.
source: As expected, CRY2-A260T binds more strongly to FBXL3 than CRY2-WT in HEK293 cells (Figure 5E), consequently leading to more ubiquitylation of the mutant protein (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CRY2-A260T has more ubiquitylation than CRY2-WT.
source: As expected, CRY2-A260T binds more strongly to FBXL3 than CRY2-WT in HEK293 cells (Figure 5E), consequently leading to more ubiquitylation of the mutant protein (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Space between Ala260 and Asp442 in FBXL3-binding form is more opened vs. the FAD-binding form.

claim: The amino acid change from Ala260 to Thr increases molecular density in the space between Ala260 and Asp442.

source: The amino acid change from Ala260 to Thr increases molecular density in this space and may alter electrostatic interactions between Ala260Thr and Asp442.

claim: CRY1 is destabilized in hCRY2-A260T mice.

claim: Any mutation manifesting the strong phenotypes seen in mutagenesis screens would almost certainly have been a selective disadvantage if they arose spontaneously in humans.
source: This is expected since the mutations that we identified are found in extant humans in the 'real world'. The circadian body clock plays crucial roles in maintaining normal physiological functions. Thus, any mutation manifesting the strong phenotypes seen in mutagenesis screens would almost certainly have been a selective disadvantage if they arose spontaneously in humans.
evidence: This is inferred from evolutionary considerations.

claim: Stabilization of CRY lengthens circadian period in mice whereas destabilization of CRY shortens the period.
source: Growing evidence indicates that stability of CRY proteins dominantly determines the circadian period length (Godinho et al., 2007; Hirano et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2013; Siepka et al., 2007; St John et al., 2014): stabilization of CRY lengthens circadian period in mice whereas destabilization of CRY shortens the period.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.
